posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
2&3) please go to the help file and read the asset standards there.
there are six different tilesheet formats, and they not only differ in size but additionally in structure as to what type of tile goes where.
Aside from regular 48x48 pixel tiles, MZ uses autotiles of 96x96 pixel, 96x144 pixel and 288x144 pixel in size. and you cannot mix those formats - A1 animated autotiles have to be placed into slot A1 and so on, only the B-E slots are interchangable.
1) pixel perfect at full screen means that you have to set the game screen size to the same numbers as your physical pixel numbers of your monitor - which additionally means that someone with a smaller monitor cannot play the game at all, while people with larger monitors will NOT be pixel perfect at fullscreen.
sorry, there is absolutely no way in any 2D game to be pixel perfect at multiple screen sizes, not without having different tileset settings  for every different screen size.
7) as part of the explanation to 2&3, you can only make tilesets in the specific size described in the help file.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
You're mixing up several different things.
a single tile in MZ is 48x48 pixel.
Which means that a 786x786 tilesheet actually contains 16x16 tiles.
But since the editor has limited space, those 16x16 tiles are displayed as 8x32 tiles in the editor window only.
if you want to display larger tiles, especially single tiles of 786x786 pixel, then it is better to go to parallax mapping and don't use the tilesets at all.
Some people like PVG have made tilesheets that are oversized, but that additionally means that you're wasting a lot of space.
and anyway, B to E are tilesheets for decoration - ground tiles should be made as autotiles in the A#-slots.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
I'm not completely sure, but it kind of sounds to me that you're doing the wrong thing entirely. You may want to look into "parallax mapping". Roughly, this means you don't save your image as a tileset (and have no size restrictions) – instead, you save it as something like "!MapName.png" in the parallaxes folder, then select it as a parallax in map settings. Note the initial
!
– that's required.
One downside of this is that you can't specify passability sections for each tile on the result – you'll need to separately handle passability using a special "parallax tileset" which is basically a blank tileset with all the settings (but, you'd substitute a tileset with symbols indicating the type of passability so you can see what you're doing while mapping).
It
is
certainly possible to do what you're doing as a standard tileset, mind you. Just remember that, as Andar said, the display of the tiles in the editor divides your image in half and stacks the two halves vertically. So, when painting it on the map, you'd have to paint the left half, then the right half.
(Also note: you can only use a tileset of that size in B through E – the A tilesets all have different sizes and are cut up in very different ways.)

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
parallax mapping in MZ does not need a plugin, only for overlay mapping you'll need a plugin.
the important rule is the correlation between map size in tiles and picture size in pixel:
map size (in tiles) multiplied with 48 pixel/tile needs to equal the picture size in pixel.
and the filename of the picture has to start with a ! to disable the parallax (movement) and make it a static background map.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
MZ can handle any number of parallaxes without a plugin.
you only need a plugin if you want to use overlay mapping.
that means that the parallax background is always a background, but if you want a picture layer above the player - that is an overlay and needs a plugin
only in the older makers (XP, VX and VXA) there is no support for parallax mapping, those will always require a script to disable the parallax movement.
But MV and MZ support parallax mapping natively without scripts/plugins.
The only problem with large parallaxes is the RAM requirements, and no plugin can change those either. Older computers sometimes have problems if the parallax map is larger than 100x100 tiles, but a modern computer with at least 16GB RAM should have no problems handling a 200x200 tiles map or larger.
(Just to understand: a parallax map needs about one or two thousand times the RAM of a tileset map)
